items.title: The Blue Economy: The World’s Quietest Economic Engine And Its Smartest Cities
items.author: Guest Author
items.content: By Alberto Onetti The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy. For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources. Alberto Onetti, Mind The Bridge The blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central. Powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea. Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge. Blue tech: A sector defying global slowdown Against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end. The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in new capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end. The drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026). Not all blue tech is the same Blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups. We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density). The result is a matrix highlighting: Transformational technologies that have a high impact and are relatively well-established. Among those, AI and machine learning, and robotics and industrial automation occupies a particular sweet spot of high impact, substantial investment and high scaleup density (more than 200 scaleups and $20 billion invested in total). High-potential disruptive technologies, with only relatively lower levels of investment and scaleup density (roughly 50 scaleups and $3 billion to $5 billion invested per cluster). Among them, the most promising ones are maritime clean propulsion and sustainable fuels, and supply chain and freight tech. The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies. Ports: the ‘smartest smart cities’ The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy? Short answer: ports. Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy. And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook. To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation. While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy. The result is a picture that shows the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy. To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units. Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges. Early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona, a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge. Notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them. Get the full story in Mind The Bridge’s report, available for free download here. Alberto Onetti is chairman of Mind the Bridge and a professor at University of Insubria. He is a serial entrepreneur who has started three startups in his career, the last of which is Funambol, among the five Italian scaleups that have raised the largest amount of capital. He is recognized among the leading international experts in open innovation and has wide experience in setting up and managing open innovation projects — venture clients, venture builders, intrapreneurship, CVCs — with large multinational companies, as well as advising and training on this subject. Onetti has a column on Sifted (Financial Times) and several other tech blogs.

items.title: Internet traffic and attacks during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections
items.author: Patrick Day
items.content: Visitors to government election websites surged 363% on November 3, the date of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States. Across Cloudflare's election protection programs, we also detected a significant shift in the types and timing of cyberattacks throughout 2026. Unlike what we saw in other recent elections, attackers focused on gaining access to internal systems and data, rather than knocking websites offline. Government election websites faced website vulnerability attempts 180 times more often than denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, and at roughly ten times the rate of Cloudflare's broader customer base. We also found evidence of at least one attempt to exploit a recently disclosed critical PHP vulnerability on a state government voting website in the Western United States. These attacks peaked in late October, several weeks before the election. Vulnerability exploit attempts climbed steadily throughout 2026: from 200,000 per day in January, to 2 million per day in October. However, on Election Day in the U.S., Cloudflare detected no escalation in attack volume and zero major DDoS incidents across protected election sites, marking a sharp contrast to other recent elections, such as in Moldova last year. Our data regarding cyberattacks on election institutions came from organizations participating in Cloudflare's free cybersecurity programs: the Athenian Project, Cloudflare for Campaigns, and Project Galileo. Together, these initiatives helped protect more than 1,400 election-related websites during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, including those belonging to state and local governments, candidates, political parties, voting-rights advocates, journalists, and civil society groups. Cloudflare launched its first election protection program in 2016 after widespread reports of cyberattacks targeting the U.S. elections. A decade later, it is remarkable to see how far governments and campaigns have come in securing their digital infrastructure. We are proud to help protect democratic institutions and are encouraged that cyberattacks were once again not a disruptive factor in 2026. In this post, we examine traffic and attacks observed against those organizations on Election Day, analyze the most common types of attacks of the 2026 cycle, and provide recommendations based on those findings. Election Day: significant voter traffic, minimal attacks Ordinary user traffic to state and local government election websites was higher on Election Day (November 3) than any other day in 2026. Traffic to those sites increased to approximately 602 million requests, up from 130 million on November 1. By comparison, traffic across the rest of Cloudflare’s global network rose by only 12% over the same period. State and local government election websites provide authoritative information to voters on how to register, where to vote, and who won. Because of their critical role, these platforms are often targeted by those seeking to suppress voter turnout, disrupt the reporting of results, or steal sensitive information. On Election Day itself, Cloudflare did not record a single significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack across any of its 1,400 election-related websites. The only significant DDoS attack occurred on November 2, targeting a candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in California and totaled 520,000 requests. By comparison, the Moldovan Election Commission experienced more than 898 million malicious requests in a single 12-hour period on their Election Day in 2025, with attacks peaking at 324,333 requests per second. Prior to Election Day: the most common attacks in the 2026 cycle Website vulnerability scans were by far the most common attack observed by Cloudflare in the 2026 U.S. election cycle. In the 12 months leading up to the election, Cloudflare mitigated 392 million such attacks on government election websites alone. Website vulnerability attacks exploit outdated or vulnerable website code to gain access to internal systems and data. For example, cross-site scripting attacks inject malicious code into web pages in order to capture administrator credentials or deface site content. SQL injection manipulates database queries allowing attackers to potentially extract voter records or alter data. Phishing and other malicious emails targeting political campaigns protected by the company occurred at rates consistent with Cloudflare's broader network, but showed signs of sophistication. In the 90 days leading up to the election, 3.9% of emails sent to organizations participating in Cloudflare for Campaigns were identified as malicious, closely tracking the 4.8 percent baseline across other Cloudflare customers. However, nearly 42% of those malicious emails managed to bypass basic email authentication checks, such as verifying sender identity or preventing in-transit tampering. These threats were nonetheless identified by Cloudflare’s advanced phishing detection tools. Although website vulnerabilities were the most common attack overall, for journalism and election-related civil society organizations, DDoS was the most common. Over the same 12-month period, Cloudflare mitigated over 10.8 billion DDoS requests targeting these groups. The largest single attack occurred on September 10, 2026, hitting a U.S.-based news organization with 3.04 billion requests. This pattern is consistent with Cloudflare research released earlier this year, which found that among all Project Galileo entities in 120 countries, DDoS were by far the most common attack seen, accounting for 81% of all attacks. PHP vulnerability On October 21, security researchers disclosed serious vulnerabilities (known as php2shell) in PHP, an open source back-end programming language used by 70% of the world's websites. The flaws reportedly could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Cloudflare deployed Web Application Firewall (WAF) protections for all customers, prior to public disclosure of the vulnerability. On October 22, Cloudflare's PHP defense was triggered more than 9,000 times on a state government election website in the Western U.S. This attack was only detected on one election-related site and appears to have been an isolated incident rather than part of a broader trend. Recommendations Cloudflare research consistently shows that individuals and organizations participating in democratic elections face significant risk of cyberattack. Data gathered during the 2026 U.S. midterm election suggests those attacks continue to evolve, occur throughout an election cycle and not only on Election Day, and can vary depending on the type of organization targeted. Based on the recent cyberattack trends in the 2026 U.S. midterms and other elections, we make the following recommendations: Prepare for surges in user traffic. Legitimate voter interest can create traffic spikes that overwhelm unprepared infrastructure and make essential election websites inaccessible. Organizations should prepare scalable, efficient infrastructure to handle Election Day traffic increases without straining budgets or staff. Maintain security protections year-round, not just on Election Day. Cyberattacks targeting democratic institutions occur across the entire election cycle, not just around voting windows. Defensive postures must remain active continuously rather than treated as a short-term, seasonal measure. Deploy automated defenses to counter rapid threats. AI has made it easier for attackers to find and exploit new vulnerabilities. Organizations should implement security services that update automatically, like managed rules, to ensure new protections deploy by default. Ensuring voters have access to reliable information about elections not only helps encourage participation and deliver timely, accurate results, but also protects voter confidence in the democratic process itself. As more officials, more institutions, and the public increasingly rely on the Internet for those services, keeping that digital infrastructure stable, secure, and accessible becomes an essential civic priority. State and local election offices, political campaigns, party organizations, journalists, and voting rights groups in need of cybersecurity services can access them from Cloudflare at no cost. Visit the Athenian Project (for state and local election websites), Cloudflare for Campaigns (for political campaigns), or Project Galileo (for civil society, democracy, and journalism organizations) to learn more about eligibility and sign up today.

items.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
items.author: Jennifer Ouellette
items.content: Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 There's something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it's the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watch other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn't watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature. The team assigned male mice randomly to three different groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training involving three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle it out from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them. The ninth day was "fight night," when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents' excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously. Read full article Comments

items.title: How Silicon Valley lost the public, with Crooked Media’s Jon Favreau
items.author: Nilay Patel
items.content: Today, I’m talking with Jon Favreau, a political commentator and cofounder of Crooked Media. You probably know Jon best from a little show called Pod Save America, which Jon started with a group of fellow Obama staffers in the wake of Donald Trump’s election in 2016. It’s now one of the most popular podcasts in the country. Since then, Pod Save America and the company created around it, Crooked, have become one of the major success stories of independent liberal media. So one of my central questions for Jon was why he thought Democrats swept the midterms earlier this month and, more importantly, why it happened now — especially after a wave of tech billionaires made big swings to the right while buying huge pillars of the information ecosystem. That’s Elon Musk buying Twitter and turning it into X, Mark Zuckerberg sucking up to Trump while tearing down Meta’s content moderation infrastructure, the Ellison family buying stakes in TikTok, turning over the leadership of CBS News and now potentially CNN while integrating Warner into Skydance… the list goes on. How did they all miss the huge swing in the mood of the public — or, more apocalyptically, fail in their attempts to control the media and thus influence the public? Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. Crooked itself is also just a fascinating business, as all creator businesses are. When we think of what you might call news creators, we tend to look to the right — after all, conservative media have been building an alternative, direct-to-consumer pipeline since the dawn of talk radio. But Jon and his fellow Crooked cofounders created a reliable template for liberal creators, and it’s working. Crooked hired its first CEO a few years ago, now offers more than a dozen original shows, and has a staff of around 100 people working on everything from live events to political advocacy. Jon tells me the subscription business has crossed 65,000 members. So of course I wanted to know how Jon feels about topics we cover a lot here on Decoder: online distribution, the platform power of YouTube, and how you balance running a media business that has to make money with a newsroom that, ultimately, has a political mission and a strong point of view. Of course, AI. Jon has turned his own podcast Offline into something close to an AI policy show this year. He has a lot of thoughts on how Congress should tackle the issue. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Jon Favreau, the co-host of Pod Save America and cofounder of Crooked Media. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Jon Favreau, you’re the co-host of Pod Save America, you’re the host of Offline. You’re also the co-founder of Crooked Media. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks for having me, Nilay. I’m excited to have you here. I’ve been on Offline with you. It was a really fun conversation. I have a million ideas about what to talk about with you. I want to talk about Crooked as a creator company in this particular moment in media. I feel like we have to start with the midterms though. The blue tsunami is here. It feels like a repudiation of the billionaires owning all the social platforms, the billionaires owning all the broadcast networks. What do you make of that? I’ve just been turning this over in my head that the media was purchased in a huge and meaningful way, and Americans said, “No, we still see through it.” I think it’s a repudiation of a government that came into power with the chief promise of bringing inflation down and making life more affordable, and it didn’t do that. If you’ve looked at the last couple of elections, people voted a party into power and they said, “Everything’s too expensive and I want stuff to be cheaper and I don’t want to be struggling. Can you do something about it?” And then either they try to do something about it or they fail to do something about it or like Trump, you don’t even try at all. You actually make life harder, and then people say, “The propaganda that’s coming out of Fox or any of these right-wing platforms doesn’t matter. I fill up my car and gas is expensive and I don’t know if I’m ever going to be able to afford a house because interest rates are up, et cetera, et cetera.” You can say whatever you want to say, but people’s lived experiences end up being more salient than the messages that they get from politics. Is it just that simple? I hate that it’s that simple. It’s just, “Gas prices are up, just throw the bums out.” But I would say the last 10 years of politics are, “Can I tweak policy into reality?” We’ve seen it happen several times. “Can I wage memetic warfare on the American public until these Republican talking points are the framework in which all further conversation must happen?” We’ve seen it happen on the left too. I think Defund the Police is a great example of a thing that just spiraled out of control and maybe turned an election. But in particular, we’re going to wake up and the Fox News machine is going to define the terms of the debate, and then we’re going to wake up and whatever’s happening on Twitter is going to define the terms of the debate. That has been how it’s worked for an awfully long time, and “the gas prices are too high” and “this war is stupid” maybe just defeated it. It works to a point, but there are certain conditions that messaging and media just can’t overcome, especially for the party in power or forever, whoever’s running the White House. The same was true with Joe Biden. Joe Biden could go out there and say, “We passed this bill. We gave money out. We gave the checks out and things are getting better and we’re just recovering from Covid. You haven’t felt it yet, but it’s getting better and look at the economic statistics.” And people just said, “No, I don’t feel that yet. So I’m going to maybe give Donald Trump another try, even though I think he’s a shitty guy and I don’t like him very much.” But maybe they remember the economy of the first term being good. We dealt with this when Obama ran and became president in 2009. They thought, “Financial crisis. Can’t stand Bush anymore. I’m going to try Obama.” And then Obama gets into office and for the first two years, the financial crisis is over, but the recession is still there. People are still out of work. So they said, “I know you passed healthcare and I know you passed the recovery act, but I still can’t find a job. The economy just still doesn’t feel great to me. So it doesn’t matter what you say you did or how great your messaging is, I don’t feel it. I’m going to vote in a Republican Congress.” It’s been like that for as long as I’ve been in politics. Is there some reason the incumbent party does not realize that saying something that sounds like “the fundamentals of the economy are strong” kills you? Because you’re describing a pattern that repeats and it’s that phrase almost exactly. Yes. That’s why we understood it once 2012 rolled around because people were still not satisfied with the economy when Obama was running for reelection and we did everything we could to make that election a choice. We acknowledged that people were still struggling and people were still in pain. We totally avoided the long list of statistics about how wonderful the economy was getting and how everyone had recovered and all that kind of stuff. We just said, “Look, things are still rough out there, but it’s a choice. This is the kind of vision Mitt Romney has for the economy and this is the vision we have for the economy. You get to pick one.” There’s a way, if you are the incumbent party in power, to still keep people on your side, but you’ve got to at least acknowledge and be honest about how people are feeling. You can’t tell people to feel a way that they aren’t feeling. You can’t tell people that a whole bunch of issues are important that aren’t the issues that matter most to them in their lives or at least to most people, which is, “Do I feel economically secure and do I actually feel safe?” That’s why people care about crime and they care about safety in their communities and then they also care about whether they can afford gas and groceries. The one issue that really struck me in that framework is surveillance. We’ve done a number of episodes about Flock cameras and AI-enabled surveillance and the idea that you can just link all the databases together and Palantir can send a drone to your house to murder you. That connects directly to safety. The CEO of Ring has been on the show and his argument is, “If I put up enough Ring cameras, I will zero out crime in certain neighborhoods.” I’ve asked him about the mechanism of how that will exactly work and the answer is that the thieves will be deterred by surveillance. It’s the same for the CEO of Flock. It’s the same argument everywhere. “If we just watch you enough, we’ll stop crime.” The American public hates this idea. There’s some limit to how much crime-stopping you want compared to how much surveillance must occur. I watched the CEO of Flock in particular try to go hard MAGA in this election cycle and use the phrase, “The radical leftists want a crime world,” or whatever it is he was saying, and it just didn’t work. That to me felt like a glimmer of a realignment where the libertarians in America were saying, “No, we still don’t want a state with this level of power,” and your classic ACLU Democrats were saying, “Yep, that’s pretty bad,” and then throw all the bumps out, like, “Just get out of here and we’ll start over.” What do you make of that? Because there are other glimmers of realignment, but that is the one that really stuck out to me. It’s interesting. I do think privacy is the other issue that affects people personally, that they can feel. But I do think that [concerning] the whole “politicians as content creators” thing, there’s a way to do it where you are participating in the circus and then there’s a way to do it that is true to yourself and your values and the story you want to tell about where the country is and where you want to take it. If that story is compelling, then it will travel and break through even in this crowded media environment. The rise of vertical video allows for that kind of storytelling in a way that we haven’t seen in a while. After Barack Obama won the Iowa caucuses, we knew that every primary night he would get primetime coverage when he won and would be able to deliver a message to the whole country because everyone would be watching because it was primary night. We really focused on those speeches. For Talarico’s campaign, and for a lot of these other Democrats now, they have a million of those moments every day, but they still have to do the storytelling in order for it to break through. The most successful candidates figured out how to do that storytelling in a really compelling way that wasn’t just “I’m going to tell a joke on Twitter” or “I’m going to do the hype reel” if I’m the House Oversight Committee. That is an effective way of getting people’s attention, but not necessarily holding their attention. If you are a politician today, you’ve got to figure out a way to get people’s attention, but then to hold it. And to hold it, you have to have a compelling story to tell. My favorite piece of election day media was Rob Sand, the governor-elect of Iowa doing the Fleetwood Mac video where he drank the cranberry juice and longboard. I thought, this is great. I don’t know what the purpose of this video is, but I’m having a good time. And maybe that’s all you needed on this day was to just channel some vibes. Then you got to actually go make some policy proposals. You have to fill potholes in New York City and then sit there and make videos about the filled potholes, which the Mamdani administration is particularly good at doing. Do you think this class of Democrats has that ability, even though they have a president who’s threatening to veto everything that they’re going to do? I do think they have the ability. They’re going to be able to communicate. They’re going to be able to have hearings when they’re holding big tech CEOs and administration officials accountable. Those will be moments. They’re going to also have moments where they get to exert power over the government funding process. I personally think we’ll be headed towards several shutdowns because that’s going to be the main mechanism for Democrats to get their way. But also for the next two years, Donald Trump and the Congress are just not going to be the main focus. The main storyline of the next two years is going to be the presidential primaries. I remember Democrats had a huge win in 2006, and then people can barely remember until the financial crisis what George Bush and the Democratic Congress were up to between 2006 and 2008, because everyone was focused on the Republican primary for president and the Democratic primary for president, because they were two wide open primaries. Once we get into 2027, you’re going to have a million primary debates on both sides. Donald Trump’s obviously going to try to insert himself into the debate by trying to play kingmaker on the Republican side so that he can continue to get attention. And God forbid there are external events and crises that we have to deal with, then everyone’s going to be paying attention to Trump and the Congress. But the machinations of what’s happening inside the Congress I think will be the secondary story of the next two years. You mentioned tech regulation. Actually, that’s where I want to end. I’ve often described hearings in Congress with tech CEOs as content capture sessions. That’s what we’re doing. Instead of Apple having the new iPhone and all the creators rushing in to take photos of it, here’s Mark Zuckerberg and all the senators are going to rush to yell at him and we all make our videos and that’s the end of that. Nothing ever seems to happen. Our audience is particularly nihilistic about it. You can yell at these CEOs all you want, but they just get their own way. There’s a lot of opportunity for oversight, particularly around AI, particularly Jensen Huang, the opportunity to do oversight over Nvidia and the Commerce Department and the FBI, whatever is happening. Boy, is there a lot of opportunity to oversight there. How do you think that looks? We cover this often from a technology lens on the show. You cover it from a political lens on Offline. What do you think this looks like? I know what I want it to look like. Because of where we are with AI development, I am more interested in oversight that actually changes the situation, that finally puts some guardrails or restrictions on the development of super intelligence, AGI, recursive self-improvement, whatever you want to call it, than just show trials where we all get to dunk on Mark Zuckerberg. My biggest concern is we don’t have time to wait for a Democratic president or even a Republican president who’s actually going to do something to regulate the development of AI because by the time we get to 2028, it feels like the horse will have well left the barn. It’s already left the barn. I’m curious, over the next two years, can Democrats and Republicans in Congress actually force some kind of regulation or at least coordination among the AI giants to stop us from going off the cliff here? If I had to point to a realignment, it’s what I mentioned at the top. Surveillance feels like a glimmer of a realignment, and then data centers and AI feel like the glimmers of a realignment. You shouldn’t just take the economy away from people. Regardless of partisan lean, I think for most people, to your point about agency, feel you can’t just do that. You have to show up and make the case. That is enough for a wholesale realignment. Those two issues are enough for these parties to totally scramble. And you’re going to get pro-business Democrats saying, “We’re going to have to do something to work with these guys.” You’re already seeing it. There’s James Talarico saying, “I wish Elon would just stay in his lane and stay out of politics, but we need him as a great businessman.” You’re seeing it on the Republican side: “We got this wrong. We need to regulate the Big Tech companies. I’m anti-data center too.” In this environment where they basically have a little less than a year to make headway before the primary cycles begin, what do you think the steps are? I worry that when I listen to a lot of these Democratic politicians and Republican politicians, all of them, there’s only a handful that seem to really understand the technology. You talk about regulation with people and they say, “Yeah, we need safeguards.” Safeguards could be anything from its effect on children and chatbots to making sure that we don’t lose human control of artificial intelligence. I feel like the cybersecurity stuff and the bio stuff — and then where recursive self-improvement goes — are the big areas where I would want to see Democrats and Republicans get together. Even if they can’t pass laws because Trump doesn’t want to do anything to hurt the AI companies because he looks at it and says, “The stock market’s tied to this, the economy’s tied to this, and I don’t want to do anything to hurt the economy and got to beat China and all that bullshit” — which is not bullshit — but you can’t answer every single concern about runaway artificial intelligence and losing control with the word “China.” Trump seems to be doing that and some other politicians as well. But he can’t anymore because there are Chinese spies. [Laughs] Right. He’ll try. He’s going to try. This is going to change the terms of this debate. An empowered set of China hawks are saying, “Look at the spies.” But even if there were no spies, they also lifted the export controls before to send the chips to China. Because of the sexy spies. It’s right there. But it was also probably in their financial interest, even if there were no sexy spies. I do think that even if you can’t get regulations passed, there needs to be even the convening power of the federal government with these companies to sit them all in a room and say, “We have to work on this together.” And international diplomacy with the Chinese. We’re not going to get out of this in one piece by Trump and Xi meeting and saying, “Yeah, it was a great meeting and we both think AI is important and we’re going to keep talking about it.” You have to actually get down into the details and the weeds here over the next two years or else I think things could get really bad really fast. I can hear our audience screaming in their cars. I can predict their YouTube comments. The YouTube AI should just start doing predicted comments. No, I’m worried it’s not going to happen. I’m with it. They’re screaming nihilism at you. They’re saying, “None of this will happen.” I worry about the same thing. I think public pressure around this is the only avenue here right now, as long as Trump’s in power. People inside the companies, people outside the companies continue to talk about this to raise the alarm, to sound the alarm on this and to tell people about the dangers. I don’t think that’s necessarily going to get us to the best place, but it’s the best chance that we have right now. My hottest election take has been that this election proved that X is irrelevant, that Elon Musk’s purchase of X is now a failure on every dimension. It’s shrunken users. He’s definitely not making as much money as even failed Jack Dorsey Twitter used to make. Again, criticism of Elon’s X is in no way praise of the Jack Dorsey Twitter. That was a poorly run company that allowed this outcome to happen, but it’s not making more money. It doesn’t have more users. And now we can see the absolute limit of its political influence. Yeah. It has outsized influence on the political debate because of all of the journalists and politicians who are on it. What we saw in the last cycle is the limits of the political debate to influence the decision of the electorate. I would connect that to the people at these companies needing to keep raising the alarm because the place where they keep raising the alarm is on X and they’re not great communicators when it comes to the public. They can’t make the case for data centers. In fact, mostly what the public hears is, “We might kill all of you.” Another anonymous researcher has surfaced to say that they’re quitting their job instead of killing you all. Now what? Do you think that there’s a better way to make that jump to make that case? Yes, because every time I see one of these posts — I just saw someone who said, “I just came from San Francisco and I’m so scared. This is crazy,” and I said, “All right” — but then there’s never a good explanation for most people as to why. What is the scary part? San Francisco is just Milwaukee with rich people. I need to make this as clear as I can. It is not as scary as people want it to be. But I do think that there is — speaking of storytelling — a storytelling function missing here where it’s great that people are speaking out and saying this is dangerous, but then you want to say, “Okay, how is it dangerous? Give us the steps from recursive self-improvement to the robots killing us all, or robots don’t have to kill us all, but [they can create] a horrible cyber attack or biological weapons.” I do think painting the picture of actually how this could affect people and continuing to sound the alarm on that and then saying, “If we did these things, we might be able to slow this down or stop it” is important too. Because if you’re just going to scare people without providing a path to how to fix the problem or how to rein it in, then eventually, it’s just going to be noise. “Oh, another person’s screaming about how we’re all going to die. What am I going to do about that?” There’s some very basic political science in here. Why we have a government is to counterbalance industry. Again, are we telling stories on social media? Abdul El-Sayed is doing political science 101 — “I’m a capitalist.” Adam Smith is like “monopoly is a danger to capitalism,” and this is eighth grade. He’s just doing eighth grade at people all the time to explain that the role of government is to constrain industry in some way or provide some sort of framework for industry to make lives better for people instead of just collecting profits. That is the role of government. AI is the ultimate collective action problem or prisoner’s dilemma, whatever you want to call it. It is why we have governments, not just a government in our country, but why we have the United Nations and an international order of countries that even if they don’t agree, even if they are adversaries, can sit down and figure things out together because there are just some problems that none of us can solve on our own. There are some set of Republicans who say, “We should go back to being free markets. We should go back to this thing.” Do you think that they are going to have any influence in this next turn? No. Fair enough. They might have influence. A lot of them have finally realized that they have lost the public on this. I was interested to hear the All In pod after the election, and Chamath Palihapitiya especially, talking about, “We thought that maybe everyone would trust that if the asset managers and the rich people did well, they would ultimately do well. That’s clearly not the case.” It’s like, “Yeah, obviously.” But I think a lot of them just didn’t realize that. That was the longest winded, most VC coded version of the voodoo economic speech I ever heard. It was. It is wild. I’m like, “You’re just getting that now? Oh, cool. Great.” “We’re just saying trickle down didn’t work again, but in this way.” Okay, that’s fine. That ecosystem is closed. It is. I’m thinking of Andrew Sullivan warning the Republican Party of epistemic closure in 2000 on his blog on The Atlantic. And now we’ve landed at a closed podcast ecosystem where I’m pretty confident everyone’s buying views for each other, just to be clear, to make it look bigger and more influential than it is. But the fever has to break there too. The CEOs can’t all just be creators. They have to run their companies and make their shareholders money and operate in a new political environment. How does that fever break? Silicon Valley has always been incredibly insular like this. Even back in the social media age, even when we dealt with them in government. I got to know some of these folks afterwards when I moved out here. They view everyone who works in government as, “Politics is just an engineering problem to solve. The fact that it’s this messy means you must be a bunch of dummies running the place.” This is the theory behind DOGE. “If we can just go in there and bring our technology and bring our brilliance, we should solve all these political problems.” But political problems are problems of the human condition. It’s people trying to figure out how to live together and divvy up scarce resources and figure out how to govern themselves. That’s really messy and you actually need some social and political expertise to do that. You can’t just be a genius coder or a capitalist and feel like this is going to solve everything. But I think for a long, long time in Silicon Valley, they’ve seen the government as just another problem to be solved by engineering or capital allocation. And it’s just not. It’s never going to be that. Politics is going to be much messier. I think it’s all of that. And then one I would add to it is they also see it as a rich source of revenue, which is why you have seen so many of them move into being defense contractors. It’s an inarguable way to get a bunch of money from the government, to say, “We will build you weapons and AI systems for blah, blah, blah.” All of them have done it regardless of their professed values. The idea that YouTube is run by a defense contractor is mind-blowing to me. I know. But it is just straightforwardly true, right? Yeah. You can see the idea that SpaceX is a defense contractor and we might turn down Starlink in Ukraine and Trump has to go on television and be like, “I have no idea what happened.” Right, and Elon’s just sitting there saying, “I can flip a switch whenever I want.” Yeah, there’s something there. Again, to come back to collective action problems and the role of government to actually control these companies and control the industry. It seems like it’s up for grabs in a way that suggests you and I should probably talk again very soon. It feels like in these next two years, that realignment, the glimmers of it that I see are either going to come true or not. I’ve been wrong before, but something about the relationship between government and the tech industry is bound to change. I agree. Jon, this has been great. What’s next for Crooked? Tell people what to look out for. We just finished Crooked Con, which was wildly successful. We had over 3,000 people to talk about the results of the election, and now we’re just trying to figure out how to cover this primary. You’re already in primary coverage? The primary has begun. Even though people have not announced their candidacies yet, by the time we get to winter, it’s going to be in full swing. So DeSantis, Rubio and JD. Ted Cruz. Oh, God. I know, and then a million people on the Democratic side. You’re already covering it. All right. I was hopeful that we would get some sincere legislative action, but we’re doing primaries. We’ll do both. It’s going to happen at the same time. I love it. Well, thank you so much for being undercover. This has been amazing. Thanks for having me. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

items.content: Hey there, I hope you’ve been doing well! 🎃 San Francisco Halloween Better late than never - here are some #PeakBayArea Halloween anecdotes. I didn’t have time to get a costume, so I used one I had from previous years: sexy cop (as you do). But I wanted to spice it up and make it timely, so I used ChatGPT to make me a Wild West Wanted poster for misbehaving AI, so I went as I guess some sort of alignment cop. First, I went to a house party with improv friends- most didn’t get the poster references. Then I hung out with some tech friends, who either loved it, who were like, “Why would you bring AI to this, it’s our one day off 💀.” Other costumes I saw: A couple’s costume: OpenAI and Hugging Face 😅 One friend had a bunch of balloons attached to his torso, and he said he was the “AI bubble.” “Don’t pop me, you’re going to crash the U.S. economy!1!” My friend Maddy Zhang dressed up as PHP2Shell. Too real. Another couple’s costume: Astra and Kimi K3 - I asked Astra if he minded that his girl was distilling him, and he was OK with it. P.S. No newsletter next week, enjoy Thanksgiving (if you celebrate)! Sponsor 📣 Ship fast. Fix What's Exploitable. Plenty of tools generate alerts. Seeing which pipeline risks are exploitable takes context. The Secure Software Delivery Toolkit is built for teams who want to ship fast without letting scanner noise set the agenda. It includes 4 practical resources in one place to benchmark your current SDLC, identify critical security gaps, and build an actionable roadmap for your software delivery lifecycle. What’s Inside: DevSecOps Security Best Practices CI/CD Security Best Practices AppSec Best Practices Cheat Sheet State of SDLC Security 2026 👉 Get the Bundle 👈 Nice, these guides sound 🔥 AppSec Phrack #73 Some of the articles that stick out to me: a profile on Halvar Flake, “Owning the Truth: Undecidability, unsound kernels, and the forging of proof”, “Reflections on Trusting AI: A Virus Inside an LLM”, “MOLE - A Binary Ninja Plugin for Static Taint Analysis”, “Backdoor attacks against Machine Learning IRL”, “A Journey Into Kernel Exploit Development in the LLM Era”, “Security is failure: Every Patch Is a Guess.” Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere Calif’s Quang Luong describes a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder (lol, what?) that allows a remote attacker with no credentials to overwrite heap memory, read it in the style of Heartbleed, and achieve remote code execution. Pre-auth RCE in Keycloak, Atlassian Jira & Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and more. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory… The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =". 😅 💡 Calif is like DJ Khaled these days: another one. Sponsor 📣 60% of orgs run dependencies published less than 24 hours ago Datadog analyzed security telemetry from thousands of organizations across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. 60% were running dependency versions published less than 24 hours earlier, the window where a compromised package like those in the Shai-Hulud campaign does its damage. Meanwhile, the median cloud service now carries four times as many high and critical vulnerabilities as it did in February. The 2026 State of Cloud Security report also covers long-lived keys for AI inference services, keyless auth in CI/CD, and AWS data perimeters.perimeters. 👉 Read the report 👈 Oof more people have to enable dependency cooldowns 😅 I always enjoy Datadog’s state of the union reports, interesting to see what trends they find. Cloud Security Tag, You’re It: Authorization Traps in AWS ABAC DEF CON 2026 talk by CrowdStrike’s Itay Saraf in which he presents a taxonomy of authorization traps in AWS Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) implementations, showing that AWS's own managed policies have had these issues. He categorizes authorization traps into three types: alterable guards (where users can modify tags to bypass restrictions), evaluation semantics (like case-sensitivity differences), and action-key incompatibility (where actions don't support specified condition keys). The Top 10 AWS Security Research of 2026 Graciously curated by Eduard Agavriloae and I think Daniel Grzelak: New AWS IAM Attack Paths and the Framework to Exploit Them by Seth Art CodeBreach: Infiltrating the AWS Console Supply Chain and Hijacking AWS GitHub Repositories via CodeBuild by Yuval Avrahami and Nir Ohfeld CloudBashing: Exploiting Free CloudShells for Mining, Networking, Exfil, and Persistence at Scale by Jenko Hwong and Chris Ryan …and 6 other awesome pieces of research, check it out! Blue Team Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition Natalie Silvanovich announces that Google Project Zero is overhauling its vulnerability disclosure policy in response to AI-accelerated threat landscapes, moving from "90 + 30" to a phased "Full X" approach: 90 days starting now, 60 days by February 2027, and 30 days by January 2028. The change eliminates grace periods and variant policies because LLMs enable near-instant patch reverse engineering (making "soak time" obsolete), dramatically increase vulnerability discovery rates (Project Zero now finds several bugs weekly in targets that previously yielded only a few yearly), and allow multiple parties to independently discover the same bugs. The policy removes severity-based exceptions and the requirement to verify fixes before disclosure, streamlining what had become an unmanageable negotiation process as vulnerability volumes surge. Black October: Lessons From the Downstream Breaches Friend of the newsletter Ryan McGeehan shares lessons from doing incident response for a number of October 2026 serial platform breaches, where compromised dev and infra platforms led to widespread credential leaks affecting their customers. He recommends three key defenses: “Full stack” network lockdown - Implementing network allow lists across the full stack (VPNs, security groups, and platform-specific IP restrictions for GitHub, AWS, Okta, etc.) which would have prevented 90%+ of the incidents he observed. Reduce and manage secrets - Reducing secrets by using TruffleHog to inventory exposed credentials, replacing them with Workload Identity Federation or role-based access, and storing remaining secrets in managers like HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager. Establish forensic-ready logging - With centralized collection, consistent formatting, and tamper-resistant retention to enable rapid incident response and customer disclosure. 💡 Highly recommend the rest of Ryan’s blog, it is 👌 AI + Security Quicklinks AI Hacking Incidents - An attempt to track cyberattacks where attackers used AI, from published reports. Currently 286 AI-assisted cyberattacks from January 2023 to November 2026. Created by my bud Daniel Miessler. Cheat Sheet: Claude Code Security Best Practices - Claude Code and other AI coding assistants are changing how fast code ships — but they're also changing what security teams need to watch for. This practical cheat sheet breaks down the real risk surfaces AI-assisted development introduces, and gives cloud security, AppSec, and platform engineers tactical steps to close the gaps.* Offsec Harness Index - An attempt to track the open-source offensive AI agent harnesses we can verify on GitHub, and to show which ones attackers are known to have run in real operations. By Daniel Miessler. *Sponsored Inside the loop: Five AI attack frameworks that never ask permission Elastic’s Mika Ayenson analyzes five agentic offensive frameworks (ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Cairn, PentAGI, and HexStrike) that use LLMs to autonomously plan and execute attacks in 2-25 second bursts, finding that none enforce authorization in code by default and three explicitly tell their models they're pre-authorized. The frameworks leave traditional telemetry (processes, web requests, API calls, sign-ins) that defenders already collect, but their speed demands pre-selecting which detections trigger automated containment, and their ability to switch infrastructure when blocked means behavior-based detections outlast those keyed on source IPs or User-Agents. Mika provides an ES|QL hunt that detects tool-family bursts by counting distinct client types (curl, Python, AWS CLI, browsers) per source IP in one-minute windows, and recommends combining any IP blocks with credential revocation, measuring tempo per identity, scoping assumed roles tightly, and removing secrets from accessible locations. 💡 Some nice diagrams, and overall good overview, I like it 👍️ Cyber Chaos Monkey: Staying ahead of security threats with AI agents Shopify’s Dan Scofield describes Cyber Chaos Monkey (CCM), an AI agent system that continuously attacks their production infrastructure using live credentials, source code, threat intelligence, past reports, and infrastructure records to find vulnerabilities before external attackers. The system uses a two-component architecture: Discovery (which uses frontier cyber models to identify potential vulnerabilities) and Sandbox (where agents exploit bugs via live requests, log analysis, and fuzzing). CCM ensures safety through containerization, egress controls, credential proxies, and a "two-person integrity" approach where a separately-aligned judge agent monitors and can instantly kill the executor agent if it violates Rules of Engagement. CCM has executed tens of thousands of offensive engagements and identified dozens of impactful findings without causing outages. Crazy Ex-Girlfriend - Face Your Fears Some women in Midtown Manhattan are supposedly stealing finance bro’s lunches then using the name on the order to look them up on LinkedIn to message them. Sign2Shell: How We Hacked Every Major Brazilian Signature Extension Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights - Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a Windows zero-day that exploits the Common Log File System (CLFS) to escalate privileges to System level by manipulating Windows Defender's antimalware engine through symbolic links. The Feed Is Fake - That “viral” song, movie, meme, influencer, and celebrity drama was probably the product of a stealth marketing campaign. ✉️ Wrapping Up Have questions, comments, or feedback? Just reply directly, I’d love to hear from you. If you find this newsletter useful and know other people who would too, I'd really appreciate if you'd forward it to them 🙏 Thanks for reading! items.title: The best things in open source are built together
items.author: Katie Liu
items.content: In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion, more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities. Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine. Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica, an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework. I attended John Maeda and Qianqian Ye’s session at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed. This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked: “What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?” John replied: “I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.” Replica, a new open-source design harness In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica, which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit. GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground John Maeda With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate. With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit. A11y Framework, a new open-source accessibility framework Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all. As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub has to offer. Ed Summers, GitHub Head of Accessibility The Open Source Accessibility Framework, created in collaboration with external contributors from the disability and accessibility communities, launched last month. It helps make accessibility an inherent part of how projects are created. It is an accountability model with four phases so developers can turn projects and accessibility goals into public, trackable progress. A core component of this is the new ACCESSIBILITY.md file, a file now visible on repository overview pages, giving a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. Read more about the ACCESSIBILITY.md file. The power of community Going back to John and Qianqian’s Universe talk, John asked: “How does an open source community keep something lasting that long? What’s the secret?” Qianqian replied: “I think the secret is one of the most obvious ones. Community.” The GitHub repo firstcontributions/first-contributions ranked fourth among the fastest-growing community projects in 2026 by contributors, helping developers take their first steps into open source. We hope you can join our open-source community: hack away at our new projects or start your own. items.title: Eight Thoughts On Anthropic’s IPO (And What Comes Next)
items.author: Alex Kantrowitz
items.content: Anthropic raised a staggering $81 billion in its IPO Thursday, selling 980,000,000 shares at $83 a piece. The company’s shares are set to hit the public markets above $100 each, with a $2 trillion valuation in sight. And so, after much debate about whether AI technology could become a real business, Anthropic just turned in the largest initial public offering in history. The IPO is not the end of the story, though, as Anthropic will now be faced with plenty of challenges ahead. On Anthropic’s IPO day, we look at what got Anthropic here, and what’s next: Speed It’s hard to overstate just how fast Anthropic went from an idea to the world’s largest IPO. In the middle of Covid, the company’s co-founders sat outdoors in a San Francisco park, planning the company’s future in chairs they brought from home. Today, it’s become one of the world’s largest companies, a testament to the rapid pace of AI progress and how quickly the new technology is changing the world. A correct bet on enterprise Early in the generative AI era, Anthropic correctly bet on enterprise use cases. The idea was that A) Tackling harder enterprise problems would force it to build smarter models, and B) Getting these problems right could be very lucrative. Anthropic made this wager before there was consensus that AI models could become smart enough to handle these types of problems. It hit on the bet. More than just an AI model company In early 2025, Anthropic was mostly an AI model company. It sold its AI via an API, and its Claude chatbot was little used. Since then, the company has transformed its business. It is now an applications company with good AI models. Hits like Claude Code have moved Anthropic upstream. The company’s future rides on growing more Claude-Code-style applications for use in industries like manufacturing, life sciences, graphic design, healthcare, and general knowledge work. Intense recent growth Since making the applications pivot, Anthropic has grown furiously. It had 1,500 customers spending $100,000 or more in December 2025 and reached 11,900 such customers by September 2026. The company grew revenue by 147% between Q1 and Q2 in 2026 (from $4.7 billion to $11.6 billion) and another 47% in Q3 ($17 billion), demonstrating solid growth even after the tokenmaxxing craze fizzled. A question of sustainability Once the initial IPO excitement fades, Anthropic’s ability to sustain its momentum will come into question. The company’s customers are still working to determine AI’s ROI, and once-flowing budgets are starting to tighten. “Cost discipline” is AI’s new buzzword after runaway token spending dominated most of the first half of this year. Challenges everywhere Anthropic will also have to fend off challengers coming from all directions: Open weight models, cheap standard models from companies like Meta that competently get the job done, and model routers that switch customers off the frontier. And then there’s the public’s opposition to AI and the data centers that power it. This won’t be easy. A sad trend for retail investors SpaceX and Anthropic have both IPO’d at valuations well above $1 trillion. Companies waiting this long to IPO means most of the upside is captured in the private markets, leaving retail investors largely out of the wealth creation picture. It’s a shame, and will likely exacerbate the criticism around AI’s impact on income inequality. Anthropic’s new dilemma Anthropic has long claimed safety as a north star, but the public markets will test that commitment. Investors who prioritize quarterly revenue and profits may have less patience than VCs with multi-year commitment to the company. And the safety vs. revenue issue could get especially thorny as models get smarter and the balance becomes harder to maintain. Subscribe now Enterprise AI Is Moving Beyond Pilots. items.title: Google will launch Android app verification requirement globally in January 2027
items.author: Ryan Whitwam
items.content: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven't registered their apps to do so soon. items.title: "You’re right"—LLMs will get climate info wrong if you ask
items.author: Scott K. Johnson
items.content: Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information. Some focused on the top results that Google surfaced (back when Google was still in the business of serving links), while others examined social media content or newspaper and TV news coverage. With large language models (LLMs) now forming a share of the public information diet, it's worth looking at how they handle climate change. But there’s no direct way for researchers to look at the information people have seen. It is served ephemerally to individual users, confined to their chat session. A study led by researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) tried to tackle this question from multiple angles, testing LLMs with different prompts and evaluating their output. They started with benchmarks of simple factual questions (benchmarks that might even be in models’ training data at this point) but also analyzed more complex interactions—including when users think they’re right to push back on an answer. CO2 Q&A LLM research often faces (no-true-Scotsman-tinged) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded. In this case, the study used 33 models, including multiple versions of the major frontier and open-weight models. The flagship frontier models used were Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT-5.6 Sol. (You can find the full list in the report.) items.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
items.content: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().
